latest_articles.title: Immersive proximity to suffering and crisis: The democratic implications of distressing virtual reality content
latest_articles.abstract: Non-fiction VR and 360-degree immersive video are widely used to depict the experiences of victimized, marginalized, and traumatized people, in both historical and contemporary contexts. Immersive VR content frequently engages topics of war and conflict, forced displacement, disability, precarity, incarceration, impact of climate change, and diverse forms of oppression and discrimination. Difficult social topics are introduced experientially, promising the audience an encounter with the lived realities of hardship, suffering, and injustice. The article argues that the democratic stakes of such uses of VR are best understood not by asking whether immersion produces empathy, but by asking what kinds of self–other relations and what kinds of agency are enacted and rehearsed through immersive proximity to suffering and crisis. Drawing on political psychology and indirect-trauma research, I show how immersive proximity to suffering and crisis can shape democratic dispositions via perceived control, threat salience, and victimhood framing. Immersive proximity to suffering and crisis may support solidarity and empathy, but it can also generate personal distress, feelings of helplessness, heightened threat sensitivity, and self-focused victimhood, which may undermine social trust, openness to pluralism, and a sense of civic efficacy. Engagement with distressing content in immersive media should enable reflective processing of difficult experiences, as well as support self–other differentiation, the sense of agency, hope, control, and efficacy, instead of leaving audiences feeling powerless and overwhelmed. The article advances a heuristic for evaluating and designing non-fiction VR depictions of suffering and crisis in ways that support democratic dispositions.

latest_articles.title: Psycho-social risk and protective factors associated with resilience in journalism
latest_articles.abstract: The polarized socio-political context is a defining feature of Macedonian society, marked by challenges such as limited transparency in political and media institutions, pressure on journalists, disinformation, and self-censorship. Reporting under such prolonged and complex conditions places considerable demands on journalists’ coping capacities and resilience. This study examines the relationship between psychosocial risk factors in the work environment and resilience among journalists in Macedonia. A field survey was conducted between March and June 2025 using the Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire (COPSOQ-III) to assess psychosocial risk factors and the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (CD-RISC-25) to measure resilience. The findings suggest that journalists identify job insecurity, organizational justice, horizontal trust, work-life conflict, quality of leadership, and emotional demands as key psychosocial risk factors. The results further indicate a moderately high level of resilience, suggesting that journalists are generally able to cope with demanding working conditions, although not without strain. Correlation analysis reveals that resilience is positively associated with protective work-related factors, including meaning of work, role clarity, possibilities for development, influence at work, and sense of community, while showing a significant negative association with job insecurity. Overall, the findings suggest that journalists’ resilience is strengthened by supportive organizational conditions and weakened by uncertainty and insecurity in the work environment. The study underscores the need to reduce psychosocial risks and enhance supportive and fair working conditions in order to sustain journalists’ resilience in the Macedonian socio-political context.
affiliations: University “Ss. Cyril and Methodius” in Skopje

latest_articles.title: The hierarchy of humanization: A theory of victim visibility in news narratives
latest_articles.abstract: Journalism frames events and distributes human recognition in public discourse, yet little is known about how narrative attention is allocated among individuals within the same event. This study introduces Victim Visibility Theory (VVT), conceptualizing news stories as systems of narrative allocation in which victims receive unequal levels of humanization. Drawing on a content analysis of 433 articles from four U.S. elite newspapers covering 52 victims across four mass shootings, it examines how identity cues, symbolic capital, and structural narrative prominence shape representation. The findings show that humanization is allocated at two levels: first between events, where whole tragedies are humanized unequally, and then within events, where editorial placement provides a second-order layer of differentiation. Victims granted headline and lead placement consistently receive expanded interpretive development, while identity attributes and symbolic capital show limited, inconsistent effects. This two-level hierarchy of humanization repositions framing in a broader model of narrative visibility and informs more equitable journalistic practice.
affiliations: Product Management, Cisco, North Carolina, USA

latest_articles.title: Stories that Make Hawks? Digital News-Based User-Generated Content and Foreign Policy Orientations Among China’s Generation Z
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines the relationships between exposure to news-based user-generated content on Bilibili and Chinese Generation Z’s support for hawkish foreign policies. Guided by the Narrative Policy Framework, a survey ( N = 688) shows that self-reported exposure to villain, hero, and mixed narrative strategies is positively associated with hawkish orientations, both directly and indirectly through national pride and national humiliation. These findings suggest that, within the highly performative and affectively embedded dynamics of social media, nonofficial actors may rely on dramatized storytelling and serve as a nonnegligible component of the broader rise of hawkishness within Chinese youth communities.

latest_articles.title: The False Will Set You Free: How Lower Courts Have Translated the Supreme Court’s Latest Falsity Doctrine into Practice
latest_articles.abstract: This study provides the first descriptive mapping of the impact of the First Amendment’s rationale for advancing truth-seeking being extended counter-intuitively to provide greater protection for intentional falsehoods. Scholarly concerns over the Supreme Court’s Alvarez ruling focused on potentially creating a doctrinal vacuum of limited guidance. The study found lower courts reflected more clarity of guidance when cases involved the sorts of historically unprotected categories of false expression targeting harm beyond falsity—but considerably less so in other types of cases where it was often “not entirely clear what level of scrutiny is appropriate for laws that criminalize lying.”

latest_articles.title: Beyond Seamlessness: Mobile AI and Situated Sense-Making
latest_articles.abstract: This commentary explores what it means for generative artificial intelligence (AI) to become mobile, as interaction shifts from screen-bound querying to AI participation in the flow of everyday situations. Rather than framing this shift in terms of access or use, it approaches mobile AI through situated sense-making, understood here in terms of the constitution of sense through ongoing activities, embodied cues, social coordination, and mobile communication affordances as AI becomes part of the situation. Starting from a café interaction staged in a promotional video for a future AI device, the commentary confronts corporate claims of seamless interaction with theoretical accounts of situated sense-making. Drawing on mobile communication studies and human–machine communication (HMC), it argues that mobile AI requires a specification of sense-making as HMC's central boundary object: not only as mutual interpretation between users and interfaces but also as a process embedded in ongoing activities and interactions. The commentary develops this argument through three interrelated aspects of situated sense-making—coordination, distribution, and stabilization—showing how mobile AI may reshape participation, redistribute epistemic authority, and steer relevance toward either shared problematization or premature closure. It thereby advances an approach to analyzing and designing embodied AI that foregrounds visible coordination, responsive alignment, and stabilization that remains open to collective deliberation.

latest_articles.title: How Personal Curation Shapes Political Engagement on Social Media? Examining The Politics of Personal Curation Model
latest_articles.abstract: Although individuals today have a wide range of media choices to engage in politics, recent investigations have revealed that many are increasingly avoiding news and disengaging from politics, especially in social media. From a user-centered perspective, few effective strategies on social media have been systematically examined to enhance political engagement. Established through the curated flows framework, this study proposes the Politics of Personal Curation (PPC) model, which offers a fresh perspective by examining how everyday mundane personal curation in social media (platform expansiveness, content heterogeneity, news attentiveness, and source belongingness curation) have significantly influences on political engagement. A preregistered study from a nationally representative panel in the United States ( N = 1,270) generally indicates that expansiveness, heterogeneity, and news attentiveness curation yield higher political engagement, whereas belongingness curation is linked to lower engagement. This study further supports that these media effects on political engagement are channeled through enhanced cognitive elaboration and moderated by cross-cutting discussion.
affiliations: New Media and Social Media Domain, The Education University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China

latest_articles.title: Human Imagery and Psychological Reactance in Persuasive Health Messages
latest_articles.abstract: Although mass-mediated persuasive messages often feature images of people, their impacts are surprisingly understudied. We tested whether attributes of human imagery influence psychological reactance to a health promotion PSA, either alone or combined with language style. Participants ( N = 1,100) viewed a message promoting sun safety that contained a forceful (vs. courteous) appeal and featured a model with forceful (vs. neutral) body language. The model’s physical characteristics (gender and skin tone) also varied. Both forceful text and forceful body language indirectly lowered protective behavioral intentions via reactance, and male-model messages had this effect for female participants. Our findings demonstrate the potential for features of human imagery to inadvertently hinder persuasion. Study results also highlight the value in measuring perceived visual freedom threat alongside traditional reactance measures. We discuss implications for reactance theory and measurement and highlight important directions for research on reactance to visuals.
affiliations: Texas State University, San Marcos, USA
University of Utah, Salt Lake City, USA

latest_articles.title: Can’t Name It, Can’t Log Off: Alexithymia and Problematic Internet-Related Behaviors: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
latest_articles.abstract: Alexithymia has been proposed as a ransdiagnostic vulnerability for behavioral addictions, but its role in problematic Internet-related behaviors (PIB) has not been quantified across phenotypes and populations. We conducted a preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses. Major databases were searched in October 2025 for studies reporting quantitative associations between alexithymia and PIB (problematic Internet, smartphone, social media, gaming use, or cyberbullying). Risk of bias was appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Random-effects models pooled correlations and standardized regression coefficients; three-level and robust-variance models accounted for multiple effects per study and examined moderators and adjustment for internalizing symptoms. Eighty-three studies met inclusion criteria; 78 independent samples ( N = 42,478; 369 effect sizes total, comprising 302 zero-order correlations and 67 standardized regression coefficients) contributed to the meta-analysis. The pooled correlation between alexithymia and PIB was r = 0.36 (95% confidence interval 0.34–0.38; I 2 = 77.6%). Associations were stronger for addictive-use PIB ( r = 0.37) than for cyberbullying ( r = 0.29), broadly comparable across world regions, and tended to be larger in adults than adolescents. In multivariable models, coefficients attenuated from about β = 0.37 to β = 0.18 after controlling for depression, anxiety, and other internalizing symptoms, but remained statistically significant. Sensitivity and publication-bias analyses indicated that the association was robust. Alexithymia shows a moderate association with PIB across age groups, partly via shared variance with internalizing psychopathology but also through unique pathways. Longitudinal and mechanistic studies should test whether targeting emotional awareness can help prevent or reduce PIB.
affiliations: Faculty of Biology, Medicine and Health (FBMH), The University of Manchester, Manchester, United Kingdom.
School of Health in Social Science, The University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, United Kingdom.

latest_articles.title: Too Much or Not Enough? The Decline of the Iconic News Image and the Adaptive Challenges of Visual Digital Journalism
latest_articles.abstract: Iconic news images have traditionally played a central role in journalistic praxis and public discourse, transcending news cycles and forming shared visual narratives. However, in contemporary digital media ecologies, single images struggle to gain traction amid multimedia storytelling, divergent editorial priorities, and dynamic platform affordances. To investigate the adaptive context of this shift, this article presents a case study of photographic reporting on the Israel-Palestine conflict from October 2023 to March 2024, analysing lead images from Al Jazeera English, The Guardian, and BBC News. While some unifying themes were evident, the outlets tended not to republish single images, instead favouring a high volume of imagery alongside multimedia content. In contrast, the viral circulation of a related AI-generated image indicates the continued importance of symbolic condensation within contemporary visual discourse. As such, the widespread circulation of this image illustrates how adaptive behaviours within a complex system can incite visual coherence outwith journalistic production. The image therefore signals a potential risk: in the absence of effective journalistic adaptation, the civic function of iconic news photographs could be displaced by epistemically synthetic imagery; loosening the connection between iconic visual symbolism and photographic witnessing.
affiliations: School of Communication, Faculty of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences, University of Stirling

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: Self-Esteem as a Shared Resource Beyond Romantic Relationships: An Extension Into Friendships and Parental Relationships
latest_articles.abstract: Self-esteem is an important factor in understanding relationship quality, for both the individual and their romantic partner. Yet, most research has focused on solely romantic relationships, neglecting other close relationships that are at least equally important for understanding humans. In the present analysis, introductory psychology students at a Canadian university and their significant other (romantic partner, close friend, or primary caregiver) completed measures of self-esteem and relationship quality ( N = 308 dyads). Actor-Partner Interdependence Model analyses replicated and extended Robinson and Cameron’s (2012) findings that the higher dyad members’ combined self-esteem, the higher the dyad-level relationship quality. Thus, self-esteem may serve as a shared resource in romantic, friend, and family relationships.

latest_articles.title: Who Verifies the Verifiers? AI, Local Knowledge Production, and Credibility in Tanzania’s 2025 Election
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how Factchecking AI tools and community-based credibility practices interacted during Tanzania’s 2025 presidential election. Using data from five regions, we analyzed 342 media materials, 87 interviews, field observations, and 22 distinct contested election events. The findings identify three forms of verification disjuncture. First, AI-assisted translation and transcription sometimes changed the meaning of politically important statements before journalists could verify them. Second, fact-checks and disputed claims often moved through different communication channels, which limited the chances that people would see the correction. Third, some communities trusted personal experience, familiar sources, and collective discussion more than professional fact-checkers. Participants judged credibility through relationships, lived experience, group discussion, humor and satire, and social accountability. These practices sometimes supported the same conclusions as institutional verification and sometimes produced different judgments. We argue that fact-checking becomes politically effective when the meaning of a claim is preserved, the correction reaches the people discussing it, and the source of the correction is recognized as credible. This explains why an accurate fact-check can still have limited public influence.
affiliations: Harvard – Berkman Klein Centre for Internet & Society

latest_articles.title: Crisis informatics, disinformation, and emergency politics
latest_articles.abstract: A key question in crisis informatics is how social media and other forms of many-to-many communication can be utilized as sources of actionable information in public emergencies. Reviewing crisis informatics literature before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic, this study finds that the issue of social media veracity took on new significance during the pandemic, as policymakers became increasingly concerned about medical misinformation and disinformation. Changes to the guidelines, policies, and business practices of social media platforms, especially X, have also presented social media studies and crisis informatics with new methodological challenges. The contribution of this article is to employ the concept of ‘emergency politics’ to unpack assumptions in the field of crisis informatics in which social media are understood mainly as resources for citizen engagement, and to discuss the ramifications of pandemic and post-pandemic developments in the social media communication space for the future of crisis informatics research. Highlighting impacts of emergency measures on the flow of information on social media platforms, the study also contributes to the critical literature on social media surveillance and freedom of expression during states of emergency.
affiliations: Dimensions of Security, Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO)

latest_articles.title: From Grassroots Sleuthing to Global Uptake: Epistemic Legitimation of Open-Source Investigations in Journalism Through Mediazona’s War Casualty Project in Russia’s War on Ukraine
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how open-source investigation (OSINV) is legitimized within journalism through an analysis of a casualty-counting project by Mediazona, an exiled independent Russian newsroom documenting Russian military deaths in Ukraine. Drawing on Mediazona’s public-facing project materials and coverage by seven international news organizations, the analysis traces how epistemic authority is established and re-anchored as the project circulates across journalistic institutions. The findings show that Mediazona constructs epistemic authority through a rich epistemic repertoire grounded in procedural rigor, radical transparency, and aesthetic sense-making. As the project gains global uptake, however, these articulations do not circulate intact. Instead, news organizations selectively mobilize elements of Mediazona’s epistemic repertoire in ways that reflect their editorial routines, epistemological commitments, audience expectations, and culturally resonant interpretive frames. In this process, Mediazona’s epistemic labor—and that of its citizen contributors, whom news organizations consistently avoid labeling “sleuths”—receives varying degrees of recognition: elevated as that of an independent outlet, absorbed into the institutional authority of international collaborators, or folded into professional routines that recast the project through a data-journalistic vocabulary and original field reporting. Taken together, the findings show that OSINV legitimation is uneven and context-dependent, shifting away from amateurist connotations toward more methodologically disciplined epistemic labor.
affiliations: Department of Communication, Appalachian State University

latest_articles.title: Public reactions on TikTok: Emotional dynamics in comments to the president of Romania's posts
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines how TikTok structures the emotional dynamics of presidential communication during the initial months of a mandate, focusing on the official account of the President of Romania. Drawing on 44 TikTok posts and 29,756 unique public comments recorded between 26 May and 27 October 2025, the study combines multilingual transformer-based sentiment analysis, change-point analysis and co-commenting network analysis. After deduplication and temporal filtering, 21,654 comments were classified. The results show a positive plurality rather than a uniformly positive baseline, alongside issue-specific negativity around economic governance, justice and public safety, security, Moldova and democratic legitimacy. Validation sensitivity checks caution against strong comment-level claims, whilst a bipartite null model shows that much co-commenting density is expected from shared participation in viral threads. TikTok is therefore interpreted as a high-co-presence environment in which episodic affective pressure emerges around salient political themes.

latest_articles.title: Defensive avoidance: How intimidating, belief-incongruent, and repetitive news disengages social media users from news
latest_articles.abstract: Social media has become a key news source worldwide, transforming how people access and consume news. Despite easy access and availability of news, many users gradually tend to disengage from news consumption. Research indicates that factors such as overload and fatigue contribute to this trend, while some psychological mechanisms remain less understood, especially in non-Western contexts. To address this, we surveyed 417 Bangladeshi social media users who consume news and tested four hypotheses. Our multiple regression analysis revealed that belief-based selective avoidance, perceived threat, and news redundancy are positively associated with news avoidance, with perceived threat being the strongest factor (β = 0.24, p p = 0.001) and belief-based selective avoidance (β = 0.10, p = 0.039) also play significant roles. Trust showed a weaker, nonsignificant effect (β = −0.04, p = 0.383). These results indicate that news avoidance reflects selective disengagement from news perceived as threatening, repetitive, or belief-incongruent. By focusing on Bangladesh, this study broadens research on social media news avoidance to the Global South. Exploring some tentative steps for news outlets, such as promoting constructive journalism and reviewing digital-friendly editorial policies, could help reduce news avoidance. Limitations remain in sampling, among others.

latest_articles.title: The Relational Costs of Asymmetric Mixed Reality Headset Use in Large Groups
latest_articles.abstract: Mixed reality (MR) technologies are increasingly used in classrooms, workplaces, and collaborative environments, yet little is known about how asymmetric headset use, that is, when some interactants wear headsets and others do not within the same group, shapes interpersonal perception. Guided by uncertainty reduction theory (URT), this study examined how headset use and familiarity jointly influence social presence, closeness, ostracism, and group interaction dynamics in face-to-face MR group collaboration. University students (N = 101) were assigned to groups of 9–10 participants to either wear a headset or not before engaging in a discussion task. Compared to participants with headsets, participants without headsets felt less close to and less present with headset-wearing partners. In contrast, headset wearers, who could see the other group members via passthrough video, did not exhibit parallel decreases. Behavioral analyses showed a crossover pattern in compromise behavior, where individuals who wore a headset compromised more in unfamiliar settings (i.e. where they rated group members less familiar) but those who did not wear a headset compromised more in familiar settings, suggesting that individuals adapt communication strategies to manage uncertainty in asymmetric MR environments. Overall, MR headsets selectively affected interpersonal connection and group dynamics.

latest_articles.title: Compressed Time, Narrow Space: The Visual-Temporal Aesthetics of Mobile Microdrama on ReelShort
latest_articles.abstract: The widespread adoption of digital platforms and mobile devices has significantly transformed audiovisual storytelling. Short-form mobile microdramas represent not only a new mode of distribution but also a narrative form that reorganizes cinematic time and space. While previous research has primarily focused on platform economies, audience engagement, and algorithmic circulation, the visual-temporal organization of mobile microdramas has received comparatively little attention from the perspective of quantitative film analysis. Addressing this gap, this study investigates how mobile microdramas reorganize cinematic form through temporal compression and spatial narrowing. A quantitative formal analysis was conducted on the first episodes of 10 ReelShort series representing different narrative tropes. The analysis examined average shot length (ASL), editing rhythm, shots per minute, shot-scale distribution, and the use of establishing shots. Shot boundaries were automatically identified using Adobe Premiere Pro's Scene Edit Detection tool, while shot scales and spatial indicators were analysed through qualitative coding. The findings show that an exceptionally short ASL of 2.31 s, together with the predominance of medium shots and the limited use of full/long shots and establishing shots, minimizes spatial exposition while privileging character-centred compositions and producing a dense visual rhythm optimized for smartphone viewing. The results suggest that ReelShort reorganizes cinematic form by simultaneously compressing cinematic time and narrowing cinematic space, extending long-term stylistic tendencies in film history while adapting them to the perceptual and technological conditions of vertically oriented mobile media.

latest_articles.title: Texting for Connection in an “Always-On” Society: Roles of Content, Availability Pressure, and Emotional Fatigue
latest_articles.abstract: Texting is the most ubiquitous form of computer-mediated communication, but its ability to satisfy relational needs in an always-on society remains under scrutiny. This study examines how message content and psychological context—specifically emotional fatigue and availability pressure—determine the relational value of texting. Analyzing 5,821 ecological momentary assessments from 112 adults, the results reveal that while texting and offline interactions positively predict connectedness, offline interactions demonstrate a meaningfully stronger effect. Within the context of texting, meaningful and affectionate interactions are associated with high levels of connectedness compared with those of small talk or practical exchanges, supporting the hierarchy of communication episodes proposed by communicate bond belong theory. Notably, neither emotional fatigue nor availability pressure significantly influences the association between texting and connectedness. These findings highlight that the relational benefits of texting are resilient to emotional fatigue and availability pressure and primarily depend on the nature of the content instead of users' psychological context.

latest_articles.title: Between Journalism and Justice: Disciplinary Humility in Open-Source Investigations
latest_articles.abstract: Open-source investigations (OSI) have become an increasingly influential method for reporting on conflict, documenting human rights violations, and supporting justice and accountability efforts. As the field has matured, OSI practitioners have increasingly operated across journalistic, legal, human rights, and technical domains, creating innovation and collaboration opportunities, but also disciplinary tensions. Despite growing scholarship on the institutionalization of OSI, less attention has been paid to how practitioners navigate overlapping disciplinary mandates. Drawing on interviews with 35 practitioners involved in OSI across journalism, human rights, law enforcement and specialized investigative organizations, this article examines how disciplinary boundaries are experienced and responded to within justice and accountability contexts. The findings show that practitioners respond to tensions between journalistic and legal norms through forms of boundary recalibration, including recognizing disciplinary limitations and restructuring investigative work. To explain these dynamics, this article introduces disciplinary humility, defined as the recognition of the limits of one’s disciplinary expertise and mandate when operating across overlapping professional jurisdictions. The article contributes to digital journalism scholarship by showing that the OSI institutionalization is shaped not only by hybridity and boundary crossing, but also by boundary recalibration through which practitioners re-examine expertise and mandates across journalistic and legal contexts.
affiliations: PhD researcher in Criminology at the Department of Law, Society and Crime, Erasmus University
Assistant Professor in Digital Media and Communication at the Media and Culture Studies Department, Utrecht University

latest_articles.title: Level up, ladies: Femininity as a total project and the rise of Queen feminism
latest_articles.abstract: Critiques of liberal feminisms are increasingly emerging from the women-led “femosphere,” calling for a revised understanding of feminism through a revaluation of femininity. This article examines one such voice: a group of social media influencers who cultivate and commercialize “queen” femininity as a lifestyle, advising women on how to “level up” their lives and attract provider-minded men. We follow 14 Finnish “queen” influencer–entrepreneurs and ask how they define and practice femininity. Drawing on digital fieldwork and content analysis of 303 Instagram captions, we show how femininity is constructed as a total and infinite project—one that extends across all fronts of life. The study further demonstrates that the cultivation of a “feminine lifestyle” is not merely a set of personal preferences but also implies a broader vision of social order. We term this ideological project “Queen feminism”: an essentialized, spiritualized, and platformed articulation of neoliberal feminism, in which the entrepreneurial ethos is (re)located in the total, perpetual, and crucially impossible project of the feminine self. Beyond analyzing a (counter)movement within feminism, this paper contributes to discussions on influencer politics by showing how the entanglement of ideological work and influencer economics may hamper collective feminist projects yet contribute to wider ideological shifts.

latest_articles.title: (Un)tidying the Account: The Emotional Cost of Hearing Untold Stories
latest_articles.abstract: In qualitative research, the researcher can be considered the research instrument, in which our positionality influences our interactions with participants and our interpretations of the data. Yet, the effect of this process on the researcher is less emphasized. In this essay, I describe the experience of writing my master's thesis about sexual assault survivors' privacy management in romantic relationships, asking how we manage these embodied experiences (and our disclosures of such) as scholars.

latest_articles.title: Data benefits? Attitudes and aspirations of recipients towards social security administrative data sharing
latest_articles.abstract: This paper outlines benefit recipients’ views towards the sharing of data that is collected about them when they routinely interact with social security services. Sharing this administrative data between public bodies promises to transform the delivery and evaluation of social security. However, there remains a lack of research into public attitudes, understandings, and aspirations for the sharing of this data, particularly from those whose data would be shared. Drawing on discussions from deliberative focus groups with 41 individuals, we reflect on the scope for increased data sharing to deliver improvements for recipients.While participants were aware of how their data is currently shared and how increased data sharing might have advantages, they expressed strong distrust in government agencies to manage their data and concerns about being placed in a position of increased vulnerability. We argue individuals’ views towards data sharing cannot be separated from their lived experiences of data systems – their data realities – which are often markedly different from system designers. We conclude by offering considerations against data systems re-introducing paternalistic policy, unintentionally, via automation – which we term ‘automated paternalism’.

latest_articles.title: From mobilization to diversion: a comparative study of wartime communication tactics of Ukrainian and Russian political elites on Telegram
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how Ukrainian and Russian political elites communicate on Telegram during the ongoing Russo-Ukrainian war. Using a dataset of Telegram public posts from 2019 to 2024, we analyze changes in communication volume, thematic content, and actor engagement before and after Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion. While the invasion triggered a massive spike in elites’ activity on Telegram in both countries—most notably among actors associated with Russia’s ruling pro-regime party—the focus of this communication diverged sharply. While Ukrainian elites initially prioritized war-related mobilization, this emphasis has declined over time. By contrast, Russian elites from the start adopted a tactic of strategic diversion, avoiding discussion of the war and shifting public attention to unrelated issues, such as crises in the West. Finally, we show that communication patterns are stratified by party size, with smaller parties specializing in narrow policy niches. These findings shed light on how political elites adapt their communication strategies in online environments during wartime.

latest_articles.title: Trust in algorithms biased appraisal and boosted affect in online dating
latest_articles.abstract: The algorithmification of social encounters is a topic of immense scholarly interest. People often form layperson beliefs about how algorithms work, which can predict how people psychologically navigate algorithmic social encounters. Online dating scholars have drawn upon correlational findings to speculate that trust in algorithms primes daters to think and feel about their dating experiences in certain ways. Within a sample of U.S. adults (N = 165), we experimentally test this speculation by manipulating participants’ trusting beliefs in the efficacy of algorithms (high vs. low), assigning them to evaluate online dating profiles drawn from the same pool, and observing whether appraisal and emotion differed between conditions. Post profile evaluation, high-belief participants perceived higher online dating success than low-belief participants. In turn, more successful participants felt more self-assured and jovial, and meanwhile less anxious or sad. Our study is the first to experimentally examine trusting beliefs in dating algorithms. Findings suggest a self-fulfilling prophecy of beliefs about algorithmic social processes and warrant more future investigation.

latest_articles.title: Children’s AI use: Developmental risks and opportunities in early and middle childhood
latest_articles.abstract: A child does not need to open ChatGPT to encounter generative Artificial Intelligence (AI). It may appear as a talking stuffed toy that asks how they are feeling today, a chatbot that answers quest...

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: Lonely in Love, Driven to Buy: How Perceived Partner Materialism Influences Loneliness and Consumption in Romantic Relationships
latest_articles.abstract: Loneliness is increasingly prevalent and carries significant consequences for well-being, yet it remains common even within romantic relationships. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory and the Discrepancy Model of Loneliness, this research conceptualizes loneliness as arising when relationships fail to satisfy individuals’ need for relatedness, resulting in perceived gaps in closeness. Moving beyond prior work on value congruence, this research examines how perceptions of a partner’s materialism are associated with loneliness, relational outcomes, and consumption behavior. Results from a survey study ( N = 546) indicate that both perceived partner materialism and personal materialism are associated with greater loneliness, suggesting that unmet expectations for closeness, not value similarity, are linked to this experience. In contrast, perceived partner materialism is related to higher relationship satisfaction only among individuals who are themselves more materialistic. Perceived partner materialism and loneliness are also associated with compulsive buying and product retention tendency, even after controlling for personal materialism. Together, the findings highlight the role of perceived partner values in shaping both relationship experiences and consumer responses to unmet relational needs.

latest_articles.title: From Utterances to Official Strategy – Strategizing as a Discursive-Material Process
latest_articles.abstract: In this paper we focus on how matters of concern emerge in the first place and how those may develop into official strategy in polyphonic strategy-making. Empirically, we use visual fiction to study strategy emergence in the TV series Borgen. Conceptually, we draw from Bakhtin’s work to track the emergence, recognition, and development of strategy utterances in Borgen to examine how some strategy utterances become part of official strategy, while others get rejected. Our findings present chains of strategy utterances regarding two strategic issues in Borgen and reveal material-discursive dynamics that were associated with those strategy utterances that eventually became part of official strategy. We contribute to prior research by showing how some strategy utterances became recognized, and eventually developed as part of official strategy, while others do not. Last, in these ways our study addresses the question of strategy emergence.
affiliations: University of Oulu Business School, Finland

latest_articles.title: “You Don’t Say Employee; You Say Colleague!”: How Strategic Vocabulary Becomes Authoritative Over Time
latest_articles.abstract: Background: When understanding strategy as communicatively constituted, it matters who or what is authorized to strategize. Purpose: This article foregrounds vocabulary as an authorizing actor. Research Design: Drawing on a case study of strategic change, it examines how strategic vocabulary—words representing an aspirational strategic direction—becomes authoritative in the sense of allowing communicative acts to participate in strategizing. Analysis: In the organization serving as a case study, a strategy team aiming to flatten hierarchies introduced less hierarchically connoted words. Taking one word as an example, I identify aspirational coupling , normative grounding, and substantial linkage as phases through which strategic vocabulary acquires authority. Results: This three-phase model illustrates how vocabulary transforms into an authorizing actor and how the vocabulary’s authority interacts with other aspects of communication such as voice and genre. Conclusions: The study provides a vocabulary perspective on authorization in strategizing and highlights how efforts to flatten hierarchies by switching vocabulary can intensify contradictions between various authorities.

latest_articles.title: Between Ideals and BoPo: Daily Associations Between Exposure to Appearance Content and Body Image Among Young Individuals with Visible Differences
latest_articles.abstract: Exposure to appearance-related content, including beauty ideals and body positivity (BoPo) elements, is linked to young individuals’ body image. Despite being challenged to develop a healthy body image, research has overlooked young individuals with visible differences. This daily diary study among a community-recruited sample of 117 Dutch-speaking (i.e. 110 Belgians, 7 Dutch) young individuals with visible differences (Mage = 25.41), therefore, examined the short-term relationships between exposure to beauty ideals and BoPo elements with/without visible differences and appearance satisfaction, and body/visible difference surveillance. Also, the moderating role of protective filtering was explored. Multilevel regression models showed that on days when participants saw more beauty ideals without visible differences, they showed less appearance satisfaction, and higher body/visible difference surveillance, compared to their typical daily exposure and body image levels. Protective filtering moderated this association: individuals high in protective filtering experienced smaller decreases in appearance satisfaction. No between- or other within-person associations emerged. These findings highlight the complexity of social media exposure for the body image of young individuals with visible differences and the value of enhancing their protective filtering.

latest_articles.title: Heterogeneities of Smartphone Use Among Chinese Urban Older Adults: A Life Course Approach
latest_articles.abstract: Drawing on a qualitative analysis of semi-structured interview data, this research adopts a life course perspective to examine how Chinese urban older adults adjust their smartphone use in response to significant life events across later life. The findings reveal that multi-level life events foster a dynamic continuum of (dis)connection. At the same time, adaptive and maladaptive use patterns coexist among Chinese urban older adults, demonstrating heterogeneity in their smartphone use. By proposing a shift from an age-as-variable approach to an aging-as-process approach, this study emphasizes older adults’ contextualized (dis)connectivity situated within life course transitions and trajectories, which reflects a negotiation between individual agency and socio-technical structures.

latest_articles.title: Why research on science communication needs more meta-analyses
latest_articles.abstract: Research on science communication has expanded and diversified. Correspondingly, an increasing number of literature reviews, handbooks, and bibliometric studies have taken stock of the field’s accumulated knowledge. However, it is still difficult to identify robust, consolidated answers to key questions on science communication—answers that may help scholars, practitioners, and decision-makers. Meta-analyses—the statistical aggregation of empirical results across multiple studies to determine average effect sizes—can provide some of those answers, complementing existing knowledge syntheses and addressing their shortcomings. Yet, meta-analyses in research on science communication are rare, whereas other disciplines are much closer to establishing a culture of meta-analyses and demonstrate the usefulness of meta-analyses for specific aspects of science communication research within and beyond our discipline. We therefore propose a meta-analytical research agenda of science communication scholarship and argue that it will increase the impact of our field in the social sciences and society.
affiliations: Strategic Communication Group, Department of Social Sciences, Wageningen University & Research, The Netherlands
IKMZ—Department of Communication and Media Research, University of Zurich, Switzerland

latest_articles.title: Television Time and Electoral Success: Evidence From the Constitutional Convention Election in Chile in 2021
latest_articles.abstract: Some democracies give all political parties free television time to level the electoral campaign playing field. Relying on a case that uses open-list proportional representation rules and where voters select individual candidates, but where free television time is assigned to party lists, we explore the association between appearing in free television ads (franja) and electoral success in Chile’s 2021 Constitutional Convention election. In this unprecedented contest, airtime was allocated to parties and lists of independents. We use an original coding of 3,157 mentions across 28 days of television ads for candidates in the four largest electoral lists (692 candidates). Candidates mentioned in ads received higher vote shares (2.9 vs. 2.2 percent) and were more likely to win seats (18.6 vs. 7.7 percent). Multivariate models show that campaign spending is more strongly associated with electoral success, but mentions in the franja have a modest but statistically significant positive coefficient. Although we cannot disentangle the potential endogeneity of being more electable and appearing in the franja, the findings highlight the importance of television time for electoral success and point to how party-controlled media exposure influences intra-list competition.

latest_articles.title: Drawing boundaries: How creative practitioners navigate precarity in AI-embedded creative work
latest_articles.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) continues to grow within creative industries, existing research has examined its implications for creative labour. However, much of this work emphasises AI’s impact on efficiency gains or creativity, offering limited insight into how practitioners adopt AI tools and negotiate human-AI boundaries in practical contexts under conditions of creative precarity. To bridge the gaps, this study applies boundary work theory to examine how creative practitioners redefine what remains distinctly human in AI-mediated creative production. Based on 21 interviews with practitioners in the UK film, gaming and live performance sectors, findings show that, in creative work, boundaries between human and AI systems are neither predefined nor passively adjusted to, but are actively shaped, expanded, and maintained in real-world settings. We argue that the adoption of AI is not a simple technical adjustment but a process through which professional value and the dynamic of creative work are reconsidered and re-constituted. Practitioners intentionally engage in boundary activities to navigate the unstable work environment associated with AI integration, enabling them to defend the role of creator. Theoretically, this study demonstrates the explanatory power of boundary work theory for understanding AI-embedded creative production and identifies that boundaries are not drawn by practitioners alone but through the interplay of technological capacities, project demands, and the legal environment. Practically, it suggests the need to redesign creative workflows and refresh professional skill sets to maintain meaningful human control while also facilitating efficient human-AI collaboration.

latest_articles.title: Hydraen narrative: Conceptualising inclusive and resistant fiction
latest_articles.abstract: Hélène Cixous reclaims the monstrous figure of the Medusa in l’écriture feminine . Discourse on feminist writing has widened to be more inclusive, though we do not yet have corresponding conceptualisation for “writing from without” that encapsulates marginalised authors and subversive texts as eloquently as Cixous does that of the feminine. This paper, arising from practice-based research in writing the hypernovel Seven Sisters Unmet , posits “Hydraen narrative” to refer to the depth and breadth of narratives written from outside and resisting the homogenising effects of dominant culture. Hydraen narratives are those that proliferate under suppression and reclaim demonised creative excess through previously termed “feminist” structures, styles, and/or content: polyvocality, lack of closure, repetition, ontological metelepsis, unnatural narrative techniques, embodiment, intra- and intertextuality, questions of family versus self, and explorations of sexuality and gender. Hydraen narrative using digital interfaces galvanises the dialectical, participatory relationship between creator and audience that can lead to social change and restored (and restorative) power.

latest_articles.title: Living a dating life, rewriting romantic scripts: Young women’s dating diaries and popular feminism on Xiaohongshu
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines how young women narrate their dating experiences on Xiaohongshu, a Chinese social media platform centered on lifestyle blogging, to explore the platformization of cultural production and emerging feminist sensibilities around romance. Drawing on textual analysis and interviews, the article reveals that dating diaries constitute a unique cultural genre that foregrounds female-centered romantic narratives, offering an alternative to hegemonic patriarchal norms. Although these narratives emphasize female autonomy and agency, they are shaped by Xiaohongshu’s cultural scripts, resulting in individualized, aestheticized, and commercialized forms of storytelling that undercut their feminist potential. We argue that these practices exemplify a localized form of popular feminism in China, marked by its ambivalence as it negotiates visibility, commodification, and political sensitivity within a commercialized and regulated digital media ecosystem.

latest_articles.title: Proximate racialisation and moral panic in Italian news discourse on maranza
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines the discursive construction of maranza through a Multimodal Critical Discourse Analysis of 36 crime-news headlines and their accompanying visual material, published by 27 Italian news outlets between 2025 and 2026. Thirty-four available static images were included in a descriptive inventory, while 10 images were subjected to close multimodal analysis. The findings show how the label operates as an already intelligible classificatory noun through which heterogeneous episodes are organised around youth deviance and public security. Verbal collectivisation, the recurrent visual de-individualisation of alleged aggressors and the salience of law-enforcement actors contribute to this construction. Explicit reference to ethnic background occurs in only one headline, while several images representing alleged aggressors activate racialised meanings through bodily, sartorial and spatial markers. This asymmetry suggests a multimodal division of discursive labour, although the pattern is not uniform across the corpus. The headline–image configurations also provide restricted social contextualisation, partly reflecting the condensed and event-oriented conventions of crime reporting. By integrating MCDA with the moral panic framework, the study shows how verbal and visual resources can reconfigure a historically established label as a recognisable contemporary folk devil across geographically dispersed news contexts.

latest_articles.title: A genealogy of conceptual confusion: Epistemological fault lines across media-ritual concepts
latest_articles.abstract: Research on media–ritual intersections deploys seven concepts: media events, media rituals, mediatized rituals, media ritualization, ritual mediatization, ritual media, and ritualized media. Their overlap generates unmarked substitution between analytically divergent registers. The slippage is a structural consequence of three epistemological tributaries (Durkheimian social theory, Carey's ritual view, and mediatization theory), each foregrounding a different dimension of the same phenomena. Genealogical analysis diagnoses four confusions: process conflated with product, unmarked shifting among power paradigms, materiality–practice divergence, and directional inversion. Three fault lines (integration vs. domination, process vs. structure, exceptional vs. everyday) constitute a meta-theoretical framework. The article advances positioned conceptual deployment: researchers specify their coordinates along all three dimensions. The seven concepts serve as a diagnostic case: concept use in communication research presupposes epistemological commitments, marked or not. An under-theorized intersection, mediatized ritualization, is advanced as a provisional theoretical proposition about how platform architectures may reshape ritualized media practice.

latest_articles.title: Climate Change Disinformation| Climate Change Disinformation—Introduction
latest_articles.abstract: In the Special Section “Climate Change Disinformation,” we examine climate-related disinformation at a transition point: It is increasingly less about denying climate science than it is about arguing against climate policy. Across six studies, the collection finds that denial of the science persists among those whose public case centers on cost and fairness. It also finds that disinformation succeeds where an audience is already disposed to accept it. In this introduction, we argue that this ongoing shift is outpacing the instruments built to address it, since arguments about policy are difficult to disprove and they largely remain beyond the reach of fact-checking or news literacy. The contributions offer researchers, practitioners, and policy makers a basis for responses that engage the politics of climate action rather than only factual claims of disinformation.

latest_articles.title: Climate Change Disinformation| Climate Denialism as a Discursive Dynamic: Truth (and Politics) Beyond Facts
latest_articles.abstract: Applying Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) methods to the online output of climate change contesters, this article examines how their discursive strategies are accommodated within counter-disinformation frameworks. Critiquing the reductive epistemology shaping such frameworks, it challenges the notion that, by endorsing “depoliticized understandings” based on unassailable scientific authority, they build democratic consensus from a factually validated decarbonization imperative. It argues that unless facts generated within the scientific paradigm are incorporated into an agonistic process within which their articulation with truth remains contingent, they cannot effectively combat climate contestation.

latest_articles.title: Climate Change Disinformation| Greenwashing and Deceptive Energy Transitions: Unmasking Socioenvironmental Disinformation and Technosolutionism in LinkedIn Ads
latest_articles.abstract: This article analyzes 4,068 advertisements from 917 companies promoted on LinkedIn with the aim of identifying greenwashing on the energy transition. Recognizing greenwashing as a form of socioenvironmental disinformation, we demonstrate how it misleads audiences about the sustainability of corporate practices. Furthermore, by drawing on the concept of technosolutionism, we discuss how the uncritical emphasis on technologies in favor of sustainability can obscure structural problems. We combined computational methods with a qualitative content analysis to map the sectors of companies and their greenwashing strategies. The results indicate that 52.7% of the ads contained signs of greenwashing, mainly characterized by the use of technical terms and vague promises. LinkedIn Ads, a business-oriented social medium, have been widely used by companies to disseminate an environmentally responsible image, often through misleading information and an emphasis on technological innovations that hide real socioenvironmental impacts.

latest_articles.title: Climate Change Disinformation| Harvesting Denial: Mapping Primary and Secondary Climate Obstruction in Brazil
latest_articles.abstract: This study conducts a qualitative, exploratory investigation of climate obstruction in Brazil. Based on a literature review and an exploratory analysis of gray literature, the study maps the key players, narratives, tactics, and institutional linkages that shape climate obstruction in Brazil. By examining how obstruction spreads across political, economic, and media spheres, the study identifies patterns that mirror and diverge from those in the Global North, particularly the United States, where obstruction has longer-established roots. The analysis also discusses the recent evolution of the phenomenon into new forms of climate obstruction. Findings show that Brazilian obstruction operates as an orchestrated ecosystem primarily sponsored by agribusiness, with practical consequences for public policy. This ecosystem gained greater prominence and institutional legitimacy during the Bolsonaro administration (2019–2022), establishing obstruction as a political force rather than a discursive norm.

latest_articles.title: Climate Change Disinformation| Seeking the Truth Among Dead Crops: Carbon Footprint Victimhood, Platformed Conspiracism, and Climate Countermovement in Turkey
latest_articles.abstract: After years of climate inaction, Turkey’s ratification of the Paris Agreement in 2021 prompted the Justice and Development Party’s discursive shift from high-carbon hegemonic agenda to green developmentalist rhetoric. This policy change provoked a backlash among conspiratorial climate-denial networks on social media. When the country’s worst-ever wildfires in 2021 were followed by wheat field fires in 2022, far-right and nationalist coalitions on X disseminated the conspiracy theory that foreign actors deliberately set these fires to undermine Turkey’s food sovereignty and engineer demographic decline under the cover of the climate agenda. Drawing on critical discourse analysis, we examine tweets from 2 major hashtag campaigns linking these fires to climate conspiracy theories. Our analysis identifies 3 interconnected motivational themes: environmental nationalism, economic injustice, and population control, each framed through a rhetoric of moral decay that sustains nationalist resentment and a discourse of victimhood.

latest_articles.title: Climate Change Disinformation| Unraveling Debunked Climate Change Disinformation and Responses to Fact-Checks: Evidence From the United States, Netherlands, and Philippines
latest_articles.abstract: Although climate change skepticism and denialism have been considered influential narratives in the contemporary digital information landscape, we know little about how such narratives are legitimized in climate change disinformation across different national settings. Against this background, this study relies on an in-depth qualitative content analysis of fact-checked disinformation in the Netherlands, the United States, and the Philippines as contrasting global cases. In addition, to explore the level of resistance to fact-checks, social media comments in response to fact-checking information were analyzed inductively. Our main findings indicate that climate skepticism was often constructed by deceptively re-interpreting, de-contextualizing, delegitimizing, or altering expert knowledge and scientific evidence. Disinformation claims and responses often used a populist logic, for which common sense and direct observations were juxtaposed to the alleged dishonesty of scientists. Responses to fact-checks mostly reinforced disinformation or challenged the fact-checker, which offers limited support for the real-life effectiveness of climate change debunks.

latest_articles.title: Climate Change Disinformation| “Everybody Wants Clean Air”: Grievances and Misperceptions in the Backlash Against Net Zero in the United Kingdom
latest_articles.abstract: Social media groups opposing net-zero policies have drawn attention for coordinating disruptive protests and employing post-truth tactics, yet the motivations behind this opposition, and the role misinformation plays in it, remain largely unexamined. To address this gap, we conducted a mixed-methods study of UK Facebook groups opposing low-emissions transport schemes. We show that the backlash is rooted in substantive policy concerns and political disaffection, which organized denial campaigns exploit through misinformation. Misinformation did not autonomously drive the backlash, but, we argue, hardened existing views, diverted attention from productive critique, and helped escalate disagreement into existential conflict, making consensus more difficult. These findings can help counter misinformation and address the underlying conditions that make it appealing.

latest_articles.title: Impacts on E-Commerce Revenue Before and During an Exogenous Shock: Site Entry Channels, Visitor Status, and Transaction Value
latest_articles.abstract: A 71-week Google Analytics panel of 24 online retailers is analyzed to explore how site entry channels, visitor status, transaction value, and lagged channel patterns relate to revenue before and during a disruptive exogenous shock (COVID-19 lockdown). Findings include that direct access and repeat visitors are consistently associated with revenue. Paid search becomes a stronger revenue pathway during disruption, whereas baseline revenue (before lockdown) is concentrated at higher ticket levels. Facebook ads are associated with first-time visitor volume but show limited immediate revenue impact. Lagged models show paid search is consistently associated with later organic search and direct access.

latest_articles.title: “Hogwarts is My Home.” The Influence of Transportation, Identification, and Emotion-Specific Personality Traits on the Perceived Sense of Heimat in Fictional Media Worlds
latest_articles.abstract: In the course of globalization, people are often uprooted from their geographical homes and satisfy their need for a sense of home (sense of Heimat) through alternative sources. Until now, fictional media worlds have hardly been studied in this context, even though fiction has been shown to satisfy social needs. The results of a stimulus-based online survey, in which participants watched an excerpt from the film “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone,” show that transportation into the fictional world and identification with Harry Potter can promote a sense of Heimat and, as a result, positive affect.

latest_articles.title: The sequential replicant effect in interpersonal sincerity: evidence from AI-mediated apology and gratitude
latest_articles.abstract: Sincerity, a core interpersonal value that mobilizes emotional resources, faces distinct challenges in AI-mediated interpersonal contexts. Extending the Replicant Effect from informational trust to interpersonal sincerity, this study examines how AIMC awareness and AI involvement cues shape sincerity judgments and subsequent relational responses. Drawing on two pre-registered, two-round studies in apology (N = 546) and gratitude (N = 561) scenarios, we found that AI involvement cues reliably reduced perceived sincerity. Primed AIMC awareness showed a more sequential influence on later no-cue evaluations through AIMC suspicion. High-ambiguity AI cues produced sequential effects only in the gratitude context. These findings suggest that hybrid human-AI authorship may reshape how interpersonal sincerity is inferred and validated, while also showing that the effects of AI cues and AIMC awareness depend on cue clarity and relational context.
affiliations: School of Media and Communication, Shenzhen University , Shenzhen, Guangdong,
Cardiff Business School, Cardiff University , Cardiff, Wales,

latest_articles.title: Quietly taking sides: The machine habitus and metaphorical framing in human and LLM-generated news
latest_articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to draft the news. These systems may frame the news differently from human journalists. In particular, it remains less understood how they handle metaphor, a potent framing tool in news discourse. Following Bourdieu’s field theory, we compare LLMs’ metaphorical framing with the journalistic habitus of human reporting in two studies of German news on Chinese investment spanning a quarter century (with 2975 metaphors from human journalism and 1924 from LLM-generated news writing), and conduct a prompting experiment across four instructions and three recent LLMs (DeepSeek V4, GPT-5.5, and Claude Sonnet 4.5) with 4877 metaphors. We find that compared to journalists that favored deliberate, evaluatively charged figurative expressions, the LLM-generated news was conventional by default, framing investment as a procedural, depoliticized process. We regard this disposition as a “machine habitus”. It proved durable across prompted years and model versions, bound to a closed set of source domains, and generative , varying under instruction only within that set. Its conceptual sources and deliberateness moved sharply with the prompt, yet showed little variation across LLMs, while its evaluative orientation tracked the prompt, with only weak differences by model origin. Across two versions of LLMs, the disposition proved more durable than the volume of metaphor it governs: the newer LLMs wrote more figuratively yet remained conflict-averse. The study contributes to debates on automation, framing, and accountability in journalism.
affiliations: China University of Political Science and Law

latest_articles.title: Reconfiguring repression: Violence against journalists in Indonesia under democratic backsliding (2014–2025)
latest_articles.abstract: Violence against journalists in Indonesia has been reconfigured as a broader system of repression under democratic backsliding. This article examines how repression adapts under such conditions by conceptualizing violence as authoritarian innovation. Repression is redistributed across forms, perpetrators, and targets, preserving deniability while maintaining disciplinary effects. Analyzing 780 documented incidents (2014–2025) from the Alliance of Independent Journalists (AJI), the study codes violence across forms (physical, digital, legal, obstruction), perpetrators (state actors, non-state actors, unknown), and targets (individual journalists, media organizations). The analysis traces violence’s longitudinal reconfiguration under democratic backsliding. Three patterns emerge. First, physical attacks persist but increasingly coexist with digital harassment and obstruction. Second, perpetrator attribution becomes increasingly opaque, with unknown actors responsible for more incidents than police or non-state actors by 2025. Third, attacks targeting media organizations rise sixfold. The findings extend authoritarian innovation and press freedom scholarship, revealing how repression adapts temporally through accumulation and layering.
